vignette: A 51‑year‑old Middle Eastern woman named Leila has spent the past decade working as a social ministry coordinator for a local church. When the intake form asked her to describe what keeps her from walking into the building on Mondays, she said she always keeps a watchful eye on the exit, makes sure no one follows her, and never allows herself to be alone in any room. That day at the office, after a brief meeting with a volunteer, she glanced at the hallway mirror, felt her heart race, and hurried back to her desk, her mind flooded with a vivid flash of a slammed door from her childhood when a caregiver had physically punished her for a trivial mistake. The sudden, vivid bodily feeling—arms braced, knees trembling—was not a mere recollection; it was the same posture her body assumed during that abuse, a bodily reenactment that immediately triggered a surge of anger and a belief that danger was imminent. The intensity of that recollection made her feel as if she were being threatened again, illustrating how her memory of the abuse directly precipitated the threat‑related response. Leila’s heightened sense of threat—her irritability that can erupt into outbursts, her false alarms that prompt her to scan for hidden dangers, and the compulsive habit of checking behind her—has become a daily driver of her behavior. After the episode at the office, she felt a wave of anxiety that she could not shake. To protect herself from the perceived danger, she stayed close to the exit, avoided any meeting that required her to be alone with a client, and postponed her work that day. The next morning she told a friend she would skip volunteer hours because “I can’t risk it; I feel like someone’s watching.” This pattern of threat‑driven avoidance demonstrates how her constant monitoring of danger leads her to disengage from her meaningful role, reinforcing the belief that the world is hostile. When Leila’s intrusive memories intrude—when she cannot put the frightening event into words and her body automatically assumes the same tense posture—she instinctively pulls her coping strategies into action. The moment she feels a sudden surge of rage on recalling the abuse, she rushes to the hallway, checks the doors, and re‑positions herself near the exit. These maladaptive strategies, triggered by the raw, nonverbal memory, keep her constantly on guard and prevent her from fully engaging in the work she loves. The memory’s vividness, coupled with the emotional sting, acts as a catalyst that brings her threat response into sharp relief, forcing her into a cycle of avoidance that feels necessary for her safety. At the same time, Leila’s persistent threat monitoring has an opposite effect on her memories. Whenever she is in the act of checking behind her, her brain is primed to notice any hint of danger, and her attention is narrowed to the present threat, making her more likely to recall the abuse in vivid detail. The fear of being attacked heightens her sense of threat, which, in turn, keeps the traumatic memory fresh and readily retrievable. Thus, her anxiety about potential danger actively pulls the event into her consciousness, reinforcing the memory’s power. The avoidance strategies Leila uses have a paradoxical influence on her memories as well. By refusing to confront situations that could trigger her, she maintains a state of hypervigilance that is constantly on standby. Whenever she is in an environment that feels safe—such as the church kitchen—her mind still flickers back to the old abuse, and she feels her body tighten in the same way it did in that room. The persistent use of avoidance, rather than allowing her to process the trauma, keeps the memory vivid and emotionally charged, creating a feedback loop that keeps her in a state of readiness for imagined threats. Now, three months into her divorce and still unable to attend her weekly meetings or volunteer, Leila feels isolated and exhausted. The last week she missed two community outreach events because she could not bring herself to be alone with the group; she feared that the person she was assigned to mentor might, like the child she was once, think of her as a threat. She finally sought therapy after a client asked her, in a gentle tone, if she was still okay after a sudden burst of anger in front of everyone. The thought that she might be failing her congregation, and the constant dread of being overwhelmed by a sudden threat, pushed her to the brink. She comes to therapy hoping to understand why her memories feel so real and dangerous, and she fears that if she cannot break the cycle, she will lose the meaningful connection she has with her community.
